newsitem.title: USA: Comdex previews Internet coming attractions.
newsitem.headline: Comdex previews Internet coming attractions.

text.p: It's that time of year again, when all of computerdom descends on the Nevada desert for five sleep-deprived days of product introductions, speeches, cocktail parties, deal making, spying, schmoozing and waiting in the world's longest cab lines.

You don't have to be into computers to have heard of Comdex, or know that the weeklong geekfest running in Las Vegas through Friday is the biggest annual showcase of new personal computer hardware and software anywhere. Chances are, if it's included in Comdex's 1.3 million square feet of exhibit space, it'll show up at computer retailers, catalogues or online stores sooner or later.

This year, the same holds true for Internet-related products and services. Comdex is packed with companies announcing new Web software or services, or unveiling upgrades to their existing online offerings. A lot of what's new is insider stuff -- software tools to help companies build better Web sites, for example -- but there's plenty to interest the average Internet user.

The biggest Internet news of Comdex could be the so-called "Internet appliances," devices that connect people to the Net via their TV sets. The jury's still out on whether consumers really want to surf this way, but that's not stopping consumer-electronics and computer companies hungry for a hit.

Of the group, Bandai Digital Entertainment plans to start selling its $499 AtWorld unit in December, along with its AtWorld.Net online access service. Similar devices are being sold or developed by WebTV, NetTV, Sega, Sanyo Electric, Samsung Electronics, Hitachi, Mitsubishi, Philips, Sony, and Zenith.

Another hardware headliner is the 56 kilobit-per-second modem, which operates at twice the speed of today's standard 28.8 kbps model. But the faster modems may not take off until the industry chooses between competing standards from Rockwell Internernational and U.S. Robotics. Both companies expect to begin shipping the devices in the next several months.

Need to log on from the road? A number of companies are showing palm-sized computers and other hand-held devices that use conventional phone lines or wireless cellular or PCS networks to pick up e-mail or scan Web pages.

One company, RadioMail, says its service will be available in several months on devices from Casio, Compaq, LG Electronics, NEC and Philips. Prices are expected to start at $19.95 a month. GoAmerica's AirBrowse service lets laptop users surf via Uniden's new Unidata wireless modem. Psion's PsiMail Internet suite works with the company's palm-top computer and includes e-mail software, a Web browser and software for dialing up CompuServe or another Internet service provider.

In the online services department, America Online, which has been battling junk E-mail in the courts and devising ways to protect subscribers from unwanted messages, said it is offering the Switchboard (http://www.switchboard.com/) phone and e-mail directory to customers. Among other things, Switchboard is known for a service called "Knock Knock," a type of caller I.D. for e-mail that lets people block their online addresses from being distributed unless they say so.

CompuServe, lately upstaged by competitors and undone by stagnating membership, is getting into the Web hosting business, offering to build and maintain companies' Web sites and using its own international network infrastructure as a base. Prodigy Services, which recently unveiled a redesigned Prodigy Internet 1.1 interface for Windows 95 users, said software will be available next week for subscribers who still use Windows 3.1 or Mac.

Other Internet service providers announced expanded ISDN (Integrated Services Digital Network) access, which is up to five times faster than 28.8 kbps modems. Earthlink, a Pasadena, Calif., Internet service provider in the middle of a public offering, will offer ISDN on 334 dial-in lines throughout North America, starting at $34.95 a month. Pacific Bell, California's local phone carrier, was expected to announce its ISDN offer later in the week.

You don't have to fly to Vegas to experience Comdex firsthand. This year, loads of Web sites are putting every speech, product announcement and titillating piece of convention-floor gossip they can find online. Here are some of the best:

-- The official Comdex Web site (http://www.comdex.com/comdex/owa/home) -- Everything you wanted to know about the convention, including lists of exhibitors and speakers, but incessant Net traffic makes it nearly impossible to get through.

-- Comdex Show Daily (http://daily.comdex.com/) -- A better bet than the official Comdex site. The online version of the official show newspaper files stories every day and includes lists and links to audio and video presentations.
-- News.com (http://www.news.com/Categories/Index/0,3,38,00.html) -- cnet, the online computer magazine, has its news team covering all Comdex bases and posting reports several times a day.
-- CRN News Radio (http://www.crnnewsradio.com coverage from trade magazine Computer Reseller News. RealAudio player software needed.
-- Comdex Webcast (http://webcast.comdex.com/) -- Live video of speeches, chats with industry pundits, spycams, etc. Webcast player software needed.
(Michelle V. Rafter writes about cyberspace and technology from Los Angeles. Reach her at mvrafter(at)deltanet.com. Opinions expressed in this column are her own.)
